# Perdition Gulch

## I.

Start with the land, because the land was here first and will be here after.

Perdition Gulch sits at the junction of two dry creek beds in the southwestern territory, thirty-one miles from the nearest railroad spur, sixty from anything that could honestly call itself a river. The elevation is four thousand two hundred feet. ---

The soil isite calcium carbonate.

No—start with what can be seen.

The soil is white. When the wind takes it, it rises in curtains that look, from a distance, like the town is on fire. The town is not on fire. The town is merely vanishing, one grain at a time, into air that has not produced rain since April of 1886. It is now September of 1887. Seventeen months. The wells still draw, but what they draw tastes of chalk and sits in the stomach likeite calcium regret.

Perdition Gulch: fourteen buildings on the main road, six on the cross street, two churches (one Methodist, one backslid), a general store, a feed lot with nothing in it, a jail with nothing in it, a cemetery with too much in it. Population as of the last honest count: eighty-three. Population as of this morning, allowing for the Sheffields leaving Tuesday and old Maren Koop finally letting go Wednesday night: seventy-nine. Small enough to know every face. Small enough that absence is a sound you can hear.

Seventy-nine people. But the number that matters is five.

---

They have no name for what they are. They do not call themselves a council, a coven, a circle, a lodge. They have no charter, no minutes, no bylaws. What they have is a root cellar beneath the Methodist church that smells of damp earth and lamp oil, and what they have is an understanding, and what they have is four abilities distributed across five bodies, and what they have is a town that, against every reasonable expectation, still stands.

Count them.

**One.** Lena Olafsdóttir, forty-seven, born in the Dakota Territory to an Icelandic mother who died naming her. Lena remembers everything. Not *well* — everything. The temperature at noon on a Tuesday six years gone. The number of stitches in a hem she glanced at through a window in 1869. The exact words a man said when he thought no one was listening, the exact pitch, the exact distance between his lips and the wall he was leaning against when he said them, the exact pattern of the grain in that wall, the exact species of beetle that had bored the third hole from the left in that grain, the exact—

Everything. She remembers everything. She has written it all down, seventeen journals, locked in a cedar trunk in a room she rents above the general store, because she learned early that a woman who quotes your own secrets back to you with perfect fidelity is a woman you will eventually try to burn. The journals are her proof to herself that she is not mad. They are also, should anyone find them, her death warrant.

**Two.** Ephraim Salt, thirty-nine. A Black man in a white territory who survived by being useful and invisible, and then discovered that his body could do something that made invisibility both easier and harder. Ephraim heals. Not others—himself. Cut him and the wound draws shut like a purse string. Break his arm and you can watch the bone set beneath the skin, can hear it, a wet grinding sound like a boot in gravel. He has been shot twice, stabbed once, trampled by a horse, bitten by a rattlesnake whose venom his blood apparently found insulting. He lived through all of it. He has lived through everything, which is its own kind of wound, the kind that does not close, the kind his body does not consider a priority.

He has learned to heal others, too, but only by touch, and only by taking their damage into himself and letting his own flesh process it. The child's fever becomes his fever, but it breaks in minutes. The rancher's shattered wrist becomes his shattered wrist, but it knits in hours. He does this rarely, carefully, at night, in houses where the patient is too delirious to report what they saw. He does not advertise. He has seen what happens to Black men in this territory who draw attention.

**Three.** Thomas Gale, eleven years old, freckled, left-handed, missing his lower right canine. Thomas hears thoughts. Not all of them, not always—the range is limited, perhaps a quarter mile, and the clarity degrades with distance, and strong emotion comes through louder than calm reflection, which means Thomas's experience of the town is largely composed of anger, lust, grief, and the particular grinding anxiety of people who owe money they do not have. He does not hear *words*, precisely. He hears intentions. He knows what a person is about to do the way you know what a sentence means before the speaker finishes it—the shape of the thought arrives whole, and the details fill in. He knew the Sheffields were leaving before the Sheffields knew. He knew old Maren Koop was dying before Maren Koop did. He knows, right now, that the Garza boy is stealing penny candy from the general store, and he knows that Mr. Partridge the shopkeeper knows too and is letting it happen because the Garza family hasn't eaten since Monday.

Thomas does not sleep well. Thomas has not slept well since he was six.

**Four and five.** Ruth and Naomi Pace, twenty-three, identical in every external measurement and in several internal ones that no measurement can reach. They share a mind. Not a *hive* mind, not a single personality in two bodies—they are distinct, Ruth harder, Naomi softer, Ruth the one who speaks first, Naomi the one who speaks last, Ruth left in the saddle, Naomi right, Ruth sugar in her coffee, Naomi black—but beneath these preferences lies a shared floor of consciousness, a continuous mutual awareness that operates below language. Ruth knows where Naomi is the way you know where your left hand is: without looking, without thinking, without effort. Naomi feels Ruth's pain as a phantom ache in the corresponding limb. When they coordinate—and they can coordinate across distances the town has not yet tested the limits of—they function as a single distributed intelligence, seeing from two vantage points, reacting with two bodies' worth of speed. They are, functionally, one person who happens to occupy two locations.

They arrived in Perdition Gulch three years ago from Missouri, claiming to be the surviving family of a minister killed by cholera. This was a lie, but it was a good lie, and they have maintained it with the competence of people who have been lying in concert since they could speak.

---

Five people. Four abilities: total recall, regenerative healing, telepathy, shared consciousness. One town.

Here is what the five have done with what they are, and here is why the town still stands:

Lena's memory has mapped every schedule, every habit, every weakness of every outlaw gang, land speculator, and railroad agent who has approached Perdition Gulch in the last nine years. She knows that the Danby brothers always water their horses at the same creek, always approach from the southeast, always send one man ahead to the saloon the night before a raid. She knows the railroad's man in Tucson files his reports on the first and fifteenth. She knows the territorial assessor's deputy drinks and talks, drinks and talks, and that everything he has said in Lena's presence since 1881 constitutes a map of the railroad's intentions precise enough to steer by.

Thomas has heard the Danby scout's thoughts in the saloon and confirmed the raid's timing. Ruth, positioned on the bluff a half mile east, has relayed this through Naomi inside the cellar to the rest of the five. Ephraim has been sent, quietly, to the homesteads in the Danbys' path—ostensibly delivering supplies, actually healing the rancher whose broken leg would have prevented evacuation. The town was empty when the Danbys arrived. The Danbys found nothing worth taking and did not return.

This is only one instance. There have been dozens. The five do not prevent all suffering—they are five people, not gods, and the drought answers to no one—but they have prevented every catastrophe that travels on human legs. Perdition Gulch should have been swallowed years ago: by violence, by the railroad, by the organized cruelty of capital, by the disorganized cruelty of desperate men. It was not. It persists. Its seventy-nine remaining residents do not know why their town has been lucky when every similar town for two hundred miles has not. They do not ask. Luck, in the territory, is something you accept the way you accept weather: without examining its machinery, for fear the examination itself will make it stop.

The system works. It is elegant, even. Five load-bearing members, four interlocking capacities, one shared purpose: keep the town alive, keep themselves hidden, maintain the equilibrium. The equilibrium requires all five. It does not have a margin. There is no redundancy. Every member is the only member who does what she does, what he does, what they do. Remove one and the system does not degrade gracefully. Remove one and the system is not a system. It is just people.

The drought deepens. The wells taste of calcium carbonate, calcium carbonate, calcium carbonate. The wind takes the soil in white curtains. The town is not on fire.

Not yet.

---

## II.

Here is what happened on the eleventh of March, 1882.

The five knew. They knew for eleven days before it happened. Thomas heard the riders' intentions first—felt them, rather, the way you feel a storm's pressure change before you see the clouds. A heavy, blurred mass of purpose moving northwest across the territory, still far enough away that the details were indistinct but close enough that the *shape* was unmistakable. Violence. Directed violence. A group of men riding toward something, and the something was the Harrelson wagon train, sixteen families, forty-one adults, twenty-three children, camped in the wash seven miles south of town, waiting for a broken axle to be repaired before continuing west.

Thomas told Naomi. Naomi told Ruth, without speaking, the way she always told Ruth—through the shared floor, the current beneath the current. Ruth told Lena, and Lena, who remembered everything, who had memorized the territorial dispatches and the movements of every armed group within two hundred miles, identified them: a militia company out of the Gila country, thirty men, riding under the pretense of enforcing settlement boundaries, actually enforcing nothing, wanting nothing, simply operating on the principle that a group of strangers camped in a wash constituted a provocation, and provocation, in the territory, in 1882, was its own license.

Eleven days. The five met in the root cellar beneath the Methodist church. The lamp was lit. The earth smelled of earth. Lena presented what she knew, and it was everything, and it was enough: the militia's route, their speed, their likely point of approach, the terrain advantages and disadvantages, the wagon train's defensive capacity (negligible—farmers, families, a few hunting rifles, no military experience, no warning). Thomas confirmed that the Harrelson group's intentions were exactly what their visible situation suggested: they wanted to fix the axle and move on. They were not hostile. They were not armed in any meaningful sense. They were, Thomas said, mostly thinking about water.

Ephraim said he could ride to the wash, position himself within the wagon camp, and when the shooting started—because it would start; Lena's recall of this militia's prior actions left no room for hope—he could move among the wounded and heal what he could. His touch, in the chaos, might not be noticed. Might. In the chaos.

Ruth said she and Naomi could split—one to the bluff overlooking the wash, one to the town—and relay real-time intelligence to the Harrelson families. Warn them. Coordinate their retreat. Tell them which direction the attack was coming from, where the gaps in the line were, where to run. Through what mechanism? someone asked. Through what plausible mechanism would a stranger on a bluff know the movements of thirty armed men in real time and relay them to people a mile away? Ruth did not have an answer. Naomi, through Ruth, did not have one either.

Thomas said he could ride out himself. Eleven years old, freckled, missing a tooth. He could ride to the camp and say he'd heard the men talking, he'd overheard a plan, the wagon train should move now, tonight, abandon the axle, go. A child's warning. Plausible. Almost plausible.

But Lena, who remembered everything, who remembered what happened to people who were discovered to be different, who remembered the Salem trials not from textbooks but from a grandmother's account that she had absorbed word-for-word at age four and could still recite in its entirety, the pauses, the breaths, the places where the old woman's voice had cracked—Lena said: And if they ask how the child knew? And if the child's warning is too precise? And if the militia, which is not stupid, which has scouts, which will notice a boy riding hard from the direction of the town—if they come to Perdition Gulch afterward and ask why a child from this town knew their plans?

And if they find out about Thomas?

And then about the rest of us?

One by one, the arguments arrived. Ephraim's presence in the camp—a Black man, suddenly appearing among white settler families the night before a massacre—would draw exactly the kind of attention he had spent his entire life avoiding. The twins' relay system required explaining how two women communicated instantaneously across a mile of open desert. Thomas's ride required explaining a child's impossible prescience. And Lena's intelligence—her maps, her predicted routes, her analysis—required explaining how a woman who had never left Perdition Gulch knew the territorial movements of thirty men with the precision of a military cartographer.

Every plan required revelation. Every revelation required trust. And trust, in the territory, in 1882, for people like them—a woman with an inhuman memory, a Black man who couldn't be killed, a telepathic child, twin women sharing a single mind—trust was another word for the pyre.

They sat in the root cellar.

The lamp burned.

Ephraim said: Forty-one adults. Twenty-three children.

Lena said: I know exactly how many.

Thomas said nothing. Thomas was hearing the wagon camp—faintly, at the edge of his range, the outermost shimmer of other minds. He was hearing a woman thinking about flour. He was hearing a man thinking about the axle, the goddamn axle, the weight of the rear quarter and how it would need to be lifted and whether the jack would hold. He was hearing a child thinking about a dog.

Ruth said: If we are discovered, we cannot protect the town.

Naomi, through Ruth, said: If we are discovered, we cannot protect ourselves.

Lena said: The town is seventy-nine—no. The town was ninety-one, then. Ninety-one people who depend on what we do without knowing we do it. If we expose ourselves for the wagon train, we lose the ability to protect ninety-one people. Permanently.

Ephraim said: Forty-one adults. Twenty-three children.

Lena said: I know. I said I know.

The lamp burned. The earth smelled of damp and oil and the faint sweetness of rot where the cellar wall met the floor. Five
